title: What to Expect – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: What to Expect – Veterinary Dermatology Center

To help us with the diagnosis and treatment of your pet, please fill out and submit our New Patient Questionnaire. You should receive this after booking your appointment. If you did not receive the New Patient Questionnaire, please let us know by calling 407-986-3376 or emailing us at info.vetdermcenter.com. Please complete this prior to your initial visit. In addition, we will contact your veterinarian to obtain medical records relating to your pet’s condition. We are able to see patients when their skin is in any condition or when they are on medication for any problems. However, certain factors may affect our ability to fully evaluate your pet; thus, we request the following:
Do not feed your pet for 8 hours before your appointment. Please DO provide water.
Do not bathe your pet for at least 5-7 days prior to your appointment.
Do not apply any topical medications to your pet’s skin or ears for at least 2-3 days prior to your visit.

Should your pet require skin testing for pollen/insect allergies, steroids (topical or oral) should not be given or applied for at least 4 weeks prior to testing. Antihistamines should also be withdrawn for 2-4 weeks prior to testing. Blood allergy testing is available if your pet cannot be without steroids or antihistamines.

A list of current and past medications your pet has received is often helpful. Please include how long the medication was given and at what dosage. If it is easier, you are welcome to bring the medications with you to your appointment.
If your pet is diabetic or has any other medical conditions, please contact us for specific instructions on how to prepare for your pet’s appointment.

title: Why a Veterinary Dermatologist? – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: Why a Veterinary Dermatologist? – Veterinary Dermatology Center

A board certified veterinary specialist is a veterinarian with advanced training in a specific discipline within veterinary medicine. His or her knowledge and skills in this area have been evaluated and recognized by a specialty organization accredited by the American Veterinary Medical Association (AVMA). Specialists are recognized as Diplomates of their specialty college.

General practitioners recognize the need for specialization and refer clients for a second opinion on difficult and unusual cases. Animals are also referred when the veterinarian realizes the diagnosis and/or treatment requires instrumentation and experience that is not generally available.

The best care for your pet is provided by mutual communication between your veterinarian and the specialist. Medical history, current therapies, and any other helpful information will be requested. A complete report will be sent to your veterinarian regarding your visit with us.

Our dermatologists will work together with your primary care veterinarian to provide the highest level of care for your pet. Remember, the act of referring exemplifies your veterinarian’s concern for your pet’s well-being and overall health.

text: Veterinary Dermatology Center consists of board-certified dermatology specialists who work together to serve as a temporary extension of the care you receive from your “Family Practice” veterinarian. In addition to standard veterinary training, each of us has completed several years of advanced training in the dermatology specialty area. This enables us to diagnose and treat conditions with the most current and advanced diagnostic and therapeutic options available in veterinary medicine.

The Veterinary Dermatology Center strives to provide the most up-to-date dermatological care for our patients in a kind, caring and professional manner. Because many of the diseases we deal with are lifelong, it is also our goal to educate our clients and spend as much time as needed to help them understand and manage their pets’ condition. We feel this helps strengthen the human-animal bond by making our patients happier, more comfortable, and therefore better pets.
When would your veterinarian consider using the Veterinary Dermatology Center?

Your primary care veterinarian is an expert at handling a wide range of preventive care medical and surgical treatment procedures. You have an ongoing relationship built on trust and respect. Sometimes a cat or dog will have a problem that requires the expertise of a specialist or the use of specialized medical equipment. For a case like this, your veterinarian may refer you to the Veterinary Dermatology Center.

title: Medical Services – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: If your pet has ear, skin or allergy issues you can feel confident turning to us. Our knowledgeable doctors and staff are prepared to handle a wide variety of dermatological conditions. Please take a look at the more detailed descriptions of medical services we offer, or call us to discuss your pet’s needs.

Skin problems are common in dogs and cats and can be caused by pollen allergies, secondary infections, hormonal disorders, or parasites such as fleas and mites. These issues can be particularly difficult to treat and should be addressed promptly.

We can often diagnose a skin problem by simply examining your pet. Some dermatological diseases or conditions do require additional diagnostic procedures to ensure a correct diagnosis. Depending on your pet’s symptoms and the results of our physical exam, we may run blood work and/or perform cytology, skin scraping, cultures or biopsies.
Contact us if you notice your dog or cat scratching excessively or if he or she develops any bare patches, scabs, scaling, redness, inflammation, lumps, or bumps.

Identifying endocrine problems as early as possible is important in dogs and cats. These serious, potentially life-threatening conditions are much more manageable when caught early, allowing us to begin proper treatment.

The endocrine system is made up of a group of tissues (mostly glands) that release hormones into the bloodstream. These hormones regulate metabolism, growth, development, and reproduction and are dispersed to different areas of the body, depending on the hormone’s function. When a hormonal balance is disturbed (by a tumor or autoimmune disease, for instance), an endocrine disorder can develop. “Hyper” refers to an excess of hormone, and “hypo” refers to a deficiency in a hormone. Treatment varies depending on the disease.
There are several common endocrine disorders found in dogs and cats:
Diabetes mellitus is caused by a deficiency in or resistance to the hormone insulin.
Hypothyroidism, which is often diagnosed in dogs, indicates that the animal has low levels of thyroid hormone.
Hyperthyroidism, which frequently affects cats, indicates that the animal has high levels of thyroid hormones.
Addison’s disease (hypoadrenocorticism) and Cushing’s disease (hyperadrenocorticism) can also affect both species, although Cushing’s disease is rare in cats.

Contact us if your pet begins panting excessively, develops any skin issues (such as hair loss or dull coat), or shows any changes in behavior, energy levels, appetite, weight, water consumption, or urination.

title: Allergy Testing – Veterinary Dermatology Center
headings: Why Skin Testing vs. Blood Testing?
text: IDAT, Intradermal skin testing (IDST), Skin allergy testing

The purpose of an IDAT is to identify the individual allergens your pet is allergic to. Your veterinarian can then recommend avoidance of those allergens when possible and also can determine which allergens should be included in your pet’s allergy vaccine.

A small rectangle is shaved on one side of the patient’s body. Approximately 50 allergens are injected in a sequential pattern. These allergens consist of various grass, weed, and tree pollens, molds, some insects, and household allergens (e.g. house dust mites). If a patient is allergic to an allergen, the specific allergen injection site will become red and swollen (hive) within 15 minutes. Most patients need a small amount of reversible sedation for the procedure in order to avoid discomfort from the injections and ease any anxiety.

The diagnosis of environmental allergies is reached by confirming the presence of appropriate clinical signs and ruling out other causes of itching e.g. food allergies, parasites, skin infections. Therefore, prior to allergy testing for environmental triggers, your veterinarian will want to rule out other potential allergies such as food allergy and flea allergy. Furthermore, your veterinarian will ensure that your pet is clear of infection at the site of the test in order to prevent any false positive reactions. Medications such as steroids, antihistamines, and fatty acids will need to be discontinued prior to allergy testing as these medications can suppress allergic reactions and result in a false negative test. The “wash out” periods are as follows:
Oral steroids (i.e. prednisone, dexamethasone, Temaril-P, etc.): 4 weeks
Topical steroids (i.e. Gen-One spray, Gentizol, Mometamax, hydrocortisone, etc.): 2 weeks
Fatty acids (i.e. fish oil, flaxseed oil, etc.): 2 weeks

Your veterinarian will formulate an allergy vaccine specifically for your pet based on the results of the allergy test. The vaccine can be made into an injectable form or as drops that are given in the mouth. Injections are usually given weekly and drops are usually given twice a day. It is important to understand that while this is the best long term therapy for your allergic pet, it can take 3-12 months to see a full response. While awaiting response to the immunotherapy, your pet may need to remain on medications to keep their allergy symptoms at bay.
Why Skin Testing vs. Blood Testing?

Unfortunately blood allergy tests have some inherent problems in their design. They were initially developed for humans and the circulating antibodies that they test for are different in dogs and cats than in people. The result is that there are a lot of false positives. In other words, the test results indicate that your animal is allergic to things that he is really not. For this reason, veterinary dermatologists opt for intradermal skin testing. However, periodically blood testing is used in special circumstances in which intradermal skin testing cannot be performed, such as:
The skin is too unhealthy to test either due to infection or severe inflammation.
Prolonged drug withdrawal for antihistamines and corticosteroids cannot be tolerated.
The dog is a show dog whose hair cannot be clipped.
The intradermal skin test (IDST) is negative, yet atopy is still suspected.

title: Food Allergy and Intolerance – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: Food Allergy and Intolerance – Veterinary Dermatology Center
Food hypersensitivity, food allergy, food intolerance, cutaneous adverse reaction to food

A food allergy is an allergic reaction to a substance in a pet’s diet. The causes of food allergy are individual allergens in the pet’s food, usually protein sources more often than carbohydrates. It is suspected that certain preservatives or food additives may elicit an allergic reaction in rare cases. A pet may be allergic to one or more substances in its food.

Dogs, cats. Any age, sex, or breed of dog or cat can develop food allergies. Food allergy is more strongly suspected if the first signs of itching start before the dog is 6 months of age or after the dog is 6 years of age.

Ingredients in some pet foods may cause an allergic reaction in hypersensitive cats and dogs. Reactions are characterized by itching and/or gastrointestinal disorders, and are usually responses to a protein or carbohydrate source in the diet. Food allergies are the third most common cause of itching, and account for about 10-15% of all allergic skin diseases in dogs.

Unlike pets with seasonal inhalant allergies, pets with food allergies tend to itch year round, and may not experience much relief from anti-itch medications. Therefore, it is essential to identify and remove the type of food that is stimulating the allergic response.
Some pets will have other allergies concurrently, such as fleabite hypersensitivity and inhalant allergies, which have severe symptoms when they are not controlled.

The only consistent sign of a food allergy is itching, which typically continues throughout the year and may fail to respond well to medications. Various skin lesions may also occur, but there is no characteristic pattern of lesions associated with food hypersensitivity. The ears, armpits, groin, and feet may be affected more commonly than other body parts. Food allergic dogs commonly present with recurrent ear infections in one or both ears. The clinical signs of food allergies in cats are more variable than in dogs. Cats may have miliary dermatitis (multiple small crusted bumps on the skin), or eosinophilic granulomas (raised, red, raw areas of skin) Vomiting, diarrhea, and more frequent but formed bowel movements can be noted in some cases.

title: Video Otoscopy – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: Video otoscopy is the use of a short, rigid endoscope that uses a video camera to transmit images to a larger screen for magnification. In order to illuminate the ear canal, the scope contains fiber optics that transmit a bright light. Video otoscopes also contain a working channel, allowing instruments and irrigation in order to obtain samples from deep in the ear canal as well as to remove debris in the ear canal.

The video otoscope is useful in diagnosing and treating ear infections and growths inside the ear. Utilizing the irrigating function on the video otoscope, the doctor can remove debris that may be deep in the ear canal. Thus, the video otoscope is valuable in many ways: it allows deep ear cleaning (removing debris adhered deep in the ear canal); it allows flushing/cleaning behind a ruptured ear drum; and it allows for diagnosing, biopsying, and removing tumors in the ear canal.

While the video otoscope may be used for routine examinations, it is most commonly employed for cleaning or diagnostic procedures on diseased ears with the patient under general anesthesia. Anesthesia is employed for the following reasons: 1) to ensure the patient is completely still while working near the ear drum in order to prevent damage to the delicate structures, 2) to protect the patient’s airway from any fluid that may flow from the ears to the throat (via the Eustachian tube) during the irrigation procedure. The safest drug protocols and patient monitoring are used during the anesthetic procedure, but no anesthetic procedure is entirely free of risk. Very rarely, patients may have unexpected, even life threatening side effects during anesthesia. Thankfully, all of these events are extremely rare.

Video otoscopy itself is a safe procedure. It is usually done as an outpatient procedure, meaning that the patient will be dropped off in the morning and returns home in the afternoon. The patient may be slightly less active the day after the procedure due to the anesthesia. Very rare side effects of the video otoscopy procedure include decreased hearing, dizziness, head tilt or difficulty blinking the eye on the affected side.

Benefits of video otoscopy deep ear procedures are that it is typically the safest, most cost effective and best method to diagnose and treat serious ear diseases. The doctors will discuss this procedure with you if they feel it is appropriate for your pet.

title: Anesthesia and Patient Monitoring – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: Anesthesia and Patient Monitoring – Veterinary Dermatology Center

Making sure our patients remain safe during surgery and other medical procedures is extremely important to us. Our team of veterinarians and veterinary technicians is skilled in using anesthesia and monitoring patients to ensure their safety and provide the most comfortable experience. Anesthesia and patient monitoring vary greatly from clinic to clinic. You can be confident that we use the most effective and up-to-date protocols. The type of anesthesia we use depends on the procedure. Some require general anesthesia, while others may only call for local anesthesia. We also closely monitor every procedure, regardless of whether it’s routine or more advanced. For more specific information on our protocols, please see the individual descriptions or contact us with any questions.

We monitor our patients closely to keep them as safe as possible during procedures that require general anesthesia. A veterinary technician will continually assess your pet’s heart and respiratory rate, blood pressure, and other vital signs to help prevent any anesthetic risk.
Please feel free to ask us about our patient monitoring protocol or any concerns you might have about your pet’s procedure. We’d be happy to discuss these matters in more detail.

For some procedures, your pet will need to be administered general anesthesia so that he or she will be unconscious and not feel pain. Many pet owners worry about their pets being administered general anesthesia. We can assure you that modern anesthesia is generally quite safe; to further lower any risk, we perform a physical examination and run blood work ahead of time to catch any underlying health issues. In addition, we follow a specific anesthetic protocol, including monitoring vital signs during the procedure, to ensure the safety of our patients.

We begin most general anesthetic procedures by administering a sedative to help the pet relax and decrease any anxiety and pain. We then administer an intravenous drug to provide complete anesthesia and place a breathing tube into the patient’s trachea (windpipe). To maintain the state of unconsciousness, we deliver a gas anesthetic in combination with oxygen through the breathing tube.
Please contact us if you have any questions or concerns about your pet receiving general anesthesia or about the procedure for which your pet is scheduled.

If your pet is having a minor surgical or diagnostic procedure performed, we sometimes use a local anesthetic to help control pain. For example, when we perform a biopsy (in which a small portion of tissue is surgically removed so it can be examined), we often use a local anesthetic. Local anesthetics cause a loss of sensation in the area where the procedure is being performed. We sometimes use a sedative and/or anxiolytic (anti-anxiety medication) in combination with the local anesthetic to keep pets calm during a procedure.
Please contact us if you have any questions or concerns about your pet receiving local anesthesia or about the procedure for which your pet is scheduled.

title: Flea Prevention and Control – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: Flea Prevention and Control – Veterinary Dermatology Center

Fleas can cause problems for pets ranging from minor to life-threatening. Not only can these parasites cause severe itching, irritation, and allergies, but they can also transmit tapeworms and diseases. Fleas can infest dogs, cats, ferrets, mice, and rats. And fleas don’t just stay on pets; they can bite people, too. For more information, contact us or see the flea article in the Pet Health Library on our site.

You don’t want these blood-sucking parasites on your pet or in your home. We can help keep them away or help you get rid of them if they’ve already found their way inside. Call us to find out how to eliminate and control fleas or to start your pet on a preventive today.

title: Tick Prevention – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: Ticks are becoming more and more prevalent in North America, and they’re now being found in areas where people and pets didn’t previously encounter ticks. These parasites aren’t just a nuisance; they can cause serious—and sometimes deadly—diseases, including Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis, and tick paralysis. Contact us immediately if your pet starts coughing or has joint pain, trouble breathing, fever, weakness, or loss of appetite, weight, energy, or coordination.

The best method for keeping ticks off your pet is by keeping your dog or cat on a tick preventive. Even indoor-only pets are at risk because ticks can hitch a ride inside on your clothing or shoes. Tick preventives are safe and highly effective at controlling ticks and the diseases they carry. Call us to get your pet protected today!

Don’t panic if you find a tick on your dog or cat, even if your pet is on a preventive. Some preventives kill ticks after they’ve come in contact with your pet. Ticks can hide easily under your pet’s fur, so as an added measure of protection, we recommend checking your pet for ticks every time your pet comes in from outside. And don’t hesitate to ask us any questions you might have.

text: What to Expect – Veterinary Dermatology Center

To help us with the diagnosis and treatment of your pet, please fill out and submit our New Patient Questionnaire. You should receive this after booking your appointment. If you did not receive the New Patient Questionnaire, please let us know by calling 407-986-3376 or emailing us at info.vetdermcenter.com. Please complete this prior to your initial visit. In addition, we will contact your veterinarian to obtain medical records relating to your pet’s condition. We are able to see patients when their skin is in any condition or when they are on medication for any problems. However, certain factors may affect our ability to fully evaluate your pet; thus, we request the following:
Do not feed your pet for 8 hours before your appointment. Please DO provide water.
Do not bathe your pet for at least 5-7 days prior to your appointment.

title: Dermatology (Skin) – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: Skin problems are common in dogs and cats and can be caused by pollen allergies, secondary infections, hormonal disorders, or parasites such as fleas and mites. These issues can be particularly difficult to treat and should be addressed promptly.

We can often diagnose a skin problem by simply examining your pet. Some dermatological diseases or conditions do require additional diagnostic procedures to ensure a correct diagnosis. Depending on your pet’s symptoms and the results of our physical exam, we may run blood work and/or perform cytology, skin scraping, cultures or biopsies.
Contact us if you notice your dog or cat scratching excessively or if he or she develops any bare patches, scabs, scaling, redness, inflammation, lumps, or bumps.

title: Endocrinology (Hormones) – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: Identifying endocrine problems as early as possible is important in dogs and cats. These serious, potentially life-threatening conditions are much more manageable when caught early, allowing us to begin proper treatment.

The endocrine system is made up of a group of tissues (mostly glands) that release hormones into the bloodstream. These hormones regulate metabolism, growth, development, and reproduction and are dispersed to different areas of the body, depending on the hormone’s function. When a hormonal balance is disturbed (by a tumor or autoimmune disease, for instance), an endocrine disorder can develop. “Hyper” refers to an excess of hormone, and “hypo” refers to a deficiency in a hormone. Treatment varies depending on the disease.
There are several common endocrine disorders found in dogs and cats:
Diabetes mellitus is caused by a deficiency in or resistance to the hormone insulin.
Hypothyroidism, which is often diagnosed in dogs, indicates that the animal has low levels of thyroid hormone.
Hyperthyroidism, which frequently affects cats, indicates that the animal has high levels of thyroid hormones.
Addison’s disease (hypoadrenocorticism) and Cushing’s disease (hyperadrenocorticism) can also affect both species, although Cushing’s disease is rare in cats.

Contact us if your pet begins panting excessively, develops any skin issues (such as hair loss or dull coat), or shows any changes in behavior, energy levels, appetite, weight, water consumption, or urination.

title: Patient Monitoring – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: We monitor our patients closely to keep them as safe as possible during procedures that require general anesthesia. A veterinary technician will continually assess your pet’s heart and respiratory rate, blood pressure, and other vital signs to help prevent any anesthetic risk.
Please feel free to ask us about our patient monitoring protocol or any concerns you might have about your pet’s procedure. We’d be happy to discuss these matters in more detail.

title: General Anesthesia – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: For some procedures, your pet will need to be administered general anesthesia so that he or she will be unconscious and not feel pain. Many pet owners worry about their pets being administered general anesthesia. We can assure you that modern anesthesia is generally quite safe; to further lower any risk, we perform a physical examination and run blood work ahead of time to catch any underlying health issues. In addition, we follow a specific anesthetic protocol, including monitoring vital signs during the procedure, to ensure the safety of our patients.

We begin most general anesthetic procedures by administering a sedative to help the pet relax and decrease any anxiety and pain. We then administer an intravenous drug to provide complete anesthesia and place a breathing tube into the patient’s trachea (windpipe). To maintain the state of unconsciousness, we deliver a gas anesthetic in combination with oxygen through the breathing tube.
Please contact us if you have any questions or concerns about your pet receiving general anesthesia or about the procedure for which your pet is scheduled.

title: Local Anesthesia – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: If your pet is having a minor surgical or diagnostic procedure performed, we sometimes use a local anesthetic to help control pain. For example, when we perform a biopsy (in which a small portion of tissue is surgically removed so it can be examined), we often use a local anesthetic. Local anesthetics cause a loss of sensation in the area where the procedure is being performed. We sometimes use a sedative and/or anxiolytic (anti-anxiety medication) in combination with the local anesthetic to keep pets calm during a procedure.
Please contact us if you have any questions or concerns about your pet receiving local anesthesia or about the procedure for which your pet is scheduled.

text: My Senior Pet Seems Healthy. Is Wellness Care Worth It? | Veterinary Dermatology Center
My Senior Pet Seems Healthy. Is Wellness Care Worth It?
» My Senior Pet Seems Healthy Is Wellness Care Worth It
Your dog still loves a walk. Your cat still has a good appetite. When your veterinarian recommends another checkup or lab testing, you may wonder, “What am I paying for if my pet seems fine?”
That’s a fair question. You deserve to understand how a recommendation could help your pet before deciding how to spend your money.
If something were wrong, would I notice?

You know your pet’s everyday habits better than anyone. That knowledge matters. But some health problems develop before pets show obvious signs, and gradual changes can be easy to overlook. A careful exam can find weight loss, muscle loss, dental problems, or changes in the heart and joints that deserve early attention.

Consider a dog who takes longer to stand or a cat who pauses before jumping onto the couch. Finding and treating pain may help them move more comfortably and enjoy familiar activities again. A wellness visit is an opportunity to discuss these changes and how you can help instead of assuming they’re just getting older.
Why come back in six months?
A year is a long gap when an older pet’s health is changing.
Checkups at least twice a year
give your veterinarian more opportunities to spot concerns sooner and adjust care. Some seniors need visits even more often.

Each visit should build on the last: comparing weight and muscle, reviewing changes at home, checking comfort, and deciding whether the care plan still fits. You learn what your pet needs now, what to watch for at home and when to check back with your veterinarian.
What will testing tell us that an exam cannot?
Your veterinarian can’t check blood sugar or kidney function simply by listening to the heart or feeling the abdomen. Different tests answer different questions:
(CBCs) look for problems such as anemia (not enough red blood cells).
assess kidney and liver health, blood sugar, and other important measures.
add information about kidney function and can reveal abnormalities such as protein or glucose.
Blood pressure and thyroid testing may also be recommended. Blood and urine tests are generally recommended every
for senior dogs and cats, with certain tests added specifically for your pet based on how they are doing at home and your veterinarian’s exam findings.
If the results are normal, was that money wasted?

Normal results are useful too. They give your veterinarian something to compare with future tests. Comparing results over time can help reveal small changes. For example, a change in a cat’s blood and urine results may show early signs of kidney trouble, even when the results are still in the normal range.

If a problem is found, earlier care may mean simpler treatment, fewer disease-related complications, and a lower risk of an unexpected emergency. That can benefit your pet’s comfort and make decisions less overwhelming for you. Testing cannot promise lower bills or prevent every illness, but it can give you better information before a problem becomes an emergency.

If my budget is limited, what matters most?

text: Screwworm and Your Pet: What to Know Before Thanksgiving Travel | Veterinary Dermatology Center
Screwworm and Your Pet: What to Know Before Thanksgiving Travel
» Screwworm And Your Pet What To Know Before Thanksgiving Travel

Holiday plans often include our pets. With New World screwworm detected in parts of the United States, this is a good time to learn the warning signs, review prevention with your veterinarian, and check travel requirements before heading out. A little preparation can help protect your pet and keep your Thanksgiving plans on track.
What is screwworm, and where is the outbreak?

New World screwworm is a fly whose larvae (maggots), burrow into living tissue. The painful infestation they cause is called myiasis. Dogs and cats can be affected, along with livestock, wildlife, and, less commonly, people. Without prompt treatment, wounds can become severe and the infestation can be fatal.

Detections have been reported in Texas, New Mexico, and Arizona, including a recent case in an Arizona dog. Most U.S. dogs and cats remain at low risk because confirmed cases are concentrated in a limited region. Pets living in, visiting, or returning from affected areas need closer monitoring. Check
How can a pet become infested?

Female flies lay eggs in wounds or around body openings, including the eyes, ears, nose, mouth, and genitals. Even small wounds, such as tick bites, can provide an opening. Surgical incisions also need protection. After hatching, the larvae feed on living tissue and enlarge the wound. Mature larvae eventually drop to the ground, where they develop into adult flies and continue the cycle.
In affected areas, check your dog or cat daily. Contact a veterinarian immediately if you notice:
A wound that grows larger, drains, or develops a foul smell.
Maggots or egg masses in a wound or around a body opening.
Repeated licking, irritation, pain, unusual tiredness, or loss of appetite.
Tell the veterinary team where your pet has recently traveled. Do not wait until you return home or until a scheduled wellness visit to have a suspicious wound examined.

Finding maggots does not automatically mean screwworm: other fly larvae can infest wounds and look similar. Your veterinarian will examine your pet and arrange collection of larvae for laboratory identification, which is needed to confirm screwworm. A prompt diagnosis helps your pet get the right treatment sooner, limiting pain and tissue damage while helping protect other animals in your community.

Care should begin promptly while confirmation is arranged. Treatment involves removing larvae, cleaning the wound, and using appropriate medication; damaged tissue may need to be removed, and pain relief is often needed. Medication alone does not replace wound care.
Prevention: medication and daily care work together

If you live in or plan to visit an affected area, ask your veterinarian about screwworm prevention before exposure. The right plan depends on your pet’s age, weight, health, and travel plans. Do not assume that every flea and tick product also prevents screwworm.
Several medications have been authorized by the FDA for both prevention and treatment in pets. This is an emergency use authorization, rather than full approval for screwworm.
Ask your veterinarian which product and schedule are appropriate, and follow the current product fact sheet. A single dose should not be assumed to protect your pet throughout a trip.
Alongside medication, take these steps in affected areas:
Check your pet daily for wounds, including scratches, tick bites, and healing incisions.
Follow your veterinarian’s instructions for cleaning and protecting wounds. Keep healing wounds protected from flies.
Reduce opportunities for injury by supervising outdoor activity and checking for sharp fencing or other hazards.
Continue wound checks even when your pet receives preventive medication, and seek care promptly for concerning changes.
Traveling for Thanksgiving? Check before you go

This is an evolving problem. Whether you’re heading across town or across a border, check whether your route or destination includes an area affected by screwworm. Contact your veterinary team early to discuss protection and any required examinations or paperwork.
Within the same state: Check with that state’s animal health department before entering or leaving an affected area. Local movement restrictions may apply even when you aren’t crossing a state line.
Between U.S. states: Check with the animal health departments in both your departure and destination states. Ask about requirements for states you’ll pass through and for your return home.

From Canada to the U.S.: Check U.S. pet entry requirements and the animal movement rules for every state you’ll visit or pass through. Also confirm Canadian requirements for bringing your pet home. Tell your veterinarian your full itinerary, including any affected areas.

Check Mexico’s current pet entry requirements and any rules for the U.S. states you’ll travel through. Before leaving, also confirm what you’ll need to bring your pet home to Canada or the United States.

Ask specifically: “Does my pet need an inspection, health certificate, preventive treatment, or movement permit for this route?” Requirements can change, so check when planning and again shortly before departure. Allow extra time around Thanksgiving, when government offices and veterinary clinics may have holiday closures.

Whether your pet joins the celebrations or stays close to home, your veterinary team can help you assess their risk and build a practical prevention plan. If you find a suspicious wound or maggots, call us right away.

text: Spooked or Serene? Learning to read your pet’s body language can create a Happy Halloween | Veterinary Dermatology Center
Spooked or Serene? Learning to read your pet’s body language can create a Happy Halloween
» Spooked Or Serene Learning To Read Your Pets Body Language Can Create A Happy Halloween
Your dog looks adorable as Batman. Your cat’s tiny witch hat is ready for its Instagram debut. But are they enjoying Halloween as much as you are?
Costumes, visitors, and ringing doorbells can make the evening overwhelming for dogs and cats. Their body language can help you decide how they prefer to celebrate.
Try these five questions to see what your pet might be telling you.
1. Does your pet actually want to be Batman?
You put a superhero costume on your dog. They stop moving, lower their head, and tuck their tail. What should you do?
A. Take a photo while they’re sitting still.
B. Leave it on until they get used to it.
C. Gently remove the costume and give them a break.
D. Add the mask to complete the outfit.
Answer: C. Gently remove the costume and give them a break.

Stillness can be misleading. A dog or cat who freezes in a costume may be frightened or uncomfortable. Freezing, a lowered posture, and a tucked tail are possible signs of distress—even when your pet isn’t struggling or making noise.

Remove the outfit calmly. Scratching or biting at clothing, refusing to move, or repeatedly trying to escape are also reasons to stop dressing up. Your pet doesn’t need to wear a costume to be part of your celebration.
2. Your dog isn’t growling. Does that mean they’re comfortable?
A visitor wearing a large mask approaches your dog. Your dog turns their head away, licks their lips, and crouches. What is the best response?
A. Give your dog space and ask the visitor to step back.
B. Encourage the visitor to pet them.
C. Wait for a growl before stepping in.
D. Hold your dog still for the introduction.
Answer: A. Give your dog space and ask the visitor to step back.

Dogs can show discomfort long before they growl. Turning away, lip licking, and crouching may signal that an interaction is becoming stressful. Read these signs together and consider what is happening around your dog; one lip lick on its own doesn’t tell the whole story.
Create some distance and let your dog decide whether to approach again. Relaxed, loose body movements are more reassuring than a tense, motionless posture.
3. Your cat has disappeared from the party. Should you bring them back?
When guests arrive, your cat crouches, flattens their ears, and retreats to a favourite hiding spot. What should you do?
A. Carry them out so they can meet everyone.
B. Ask guests to offer attention in their hiding spot.
C. Block the hiding spot so they stay nearby.
D. Let them retreat and ask guests to leave them alone.
Answer: D. Let them retreat and ask guests to leave them alone.
Crouching and flattened ears can signal distress. Cats also use hiding places to feel safer when anxious or threatened. A retreat gives your cat a way to manage an uncomfortable situation.
Before visitors arrive, prepare a familiar, quiet room with a hiding place, comfortable bedding, water, and a litter box. Let your cat settle there and keep guests from disturbing them.
4. When is a festive bandana a better choice?
Your pet dislikes a full costume but is comfortable wearing their usual collar. Which option best puts their comfort first?
A. Keep the costume on for shorter photo sessions.
B. Try a simple bandana later, only if they remain comfortable.
C. Hold them while someone takes a quick picture.
D. Choose a tighter costume so it moves less.
Answer: B. Try a simple bandana later, only if they remain comfortable.
A lightweight bandana may be less intrusive than a full outfit, but your pet’s response still matters. Give them a break first and skip accessories altogether if they show discomfort.

Any clothing should allow normal movement, breathing, vision, and hearing. Avoid dangling decorations or parts your pet could swallow and supervise them while wearing it. Remove a bandana if they paw at it, chew it, freeze, or try to get away.
5. Your pet usually loves visitors. Should they greet every trick-or-treater?
Your normally social pet begins pacing and startling each time the doorbell rings. What is the best plan?
A. Keep them at the door because they usually enjoy company.
B. Ask more visitors to give them attention.
C. Move them to a familiar quiet space and reduce the interruptions.
D. Wait until they hide or growl before changing anything.
Answer: C. Move them to a familiar quiet space and reduce the interruptions.

Even outgoing pets can find repeated noise and unfamiliar visitors overwhelming. Plan around how your pet feels that evening. A secure room away from the door can reduce disturbance and help prevent escapes.
You can also hand out candy outside so visitors don’t need to ring the bell.

Halloween gives you a chance to practise a skill that matters every day: noticing your pet’s signals and responding appropriately. Whether they enjoy a brief greeting, a comfortable bandana, or an evening in their favourite hiding spot, let their comfort guide the celebration. If your pet has a history of intense Halloween fear, speak with your veterinarian beforehand about a plan to help them cope.

headings: More Treats, Fewer Tricks: A Safe Halloween with Your Pet
Decorate with Curious Pets in Mind

text: More Treats, Fewer Tricks: A Safe Halloween with Your Pet | Veterinary Dermatology Center
More Treats, Fewer Tricks: A Safe Halloween with Your Pet
» More Treats Fewer Tricks A Safe Halloween With Your Pet

From creative costumes to glowing pumpkins, Halloween brings plenty of fun—but some traditions can be frightening or unsafe for pets. A little preparation can help you enjoy the celebrations while keeping your furry friend comfortable and secure.

That taco costume may be hard to resist, but your pet might be less enthusiastic! Before dressing them up, consider their comfort and safety. Choose an outfit that fits properly and allows them to move, breathe, see, and hear freely. Avoid loose pieces or small decorations that could become choking hazards if chewed off.

Frequent yawning, lip licking, or attempts to shake or scratch off the costume may mean your pet is uncomfortable. If they seem stressed, remove the outfit. A simple festive bandana may be a more comfortable choice—if your pet enjoys wearing one.

Halloween treats belong in human hands, away from curious paws. Chocolate can be toxic to dogs and cats. Raisins are also a poisoning risk, and xylitol—a sweetener found in some sugar-free candy—is especially dangerous for dogs. Even candy wrappers can cause trouble if swallowed, including intestinal blockages.

Give your pet a treat of their own, such as a pet-friendly snack or a small amount of plain pumpkin puree (not pumpkin pie filling). Remind children and visitors to keep their candy to themselves, no matter how convincing those pleading eyes may be!
Decorate with Curious Pets in Mind

A flickering pumpkin or dangling decoration can be tempting to investigate. Unfortunately, a pet can knock over a jack-o’-lantern with a lit candle, causing burns or starting a fire. Glow sticks are generally considered nontoxic, but their contents can cause excessive drooling or vomiting if a pet bites into them.
Keep potentially hazardous decorations out of reach. Use battery-operated candles in pumpkins, and secure hanging decorations and artificial cobwebs so pets cannot become tangled in them.

Doorbells, unfamiliar visitors, and unusual costumes can make Halloween overwhelming for pets. Give them a quiet, secure room where they can settle away from the activity. Their favorite blanket, a few toys, and soft music can help create a comfortable retreat.

For pets that are sensitive to noise, a calming vest or pheromone diffuser may be worth discussing with your veterinarian. If your pet tends to become very anxious, contact your veterinary team before Halloween to ask about suitable anxiety-management options.
Watch for signs of stress, such as pacing, panting, hiding, or excessive drooling. If your pet seems uneasy, give them space and keep the festivities away from their retreat.
Keep the Front Door from Becoming an Escape Route

With the door opening repeatedly for trick-or-treaters, pets have plenty of opportunities to slip outside. Keep them indoors and away from the entrance. Gates, crates, or closed doors can help keep them secure while you greet visitors.

Check that your pet’s ID tags show your current contact information. If they are not microchipped, consider arranging it before Halloween. Take a recent photo, too, so you have one ready if they go missing. An up-to-date ID tag can help someone contact you quickly if they find your pet.

Whether your pet enjoys a comfortable costume or prefers a quiet evening in their favorite spot, let their comfort guide your plans. With a little care, you can help make Halloween a treat for everyone—furry family members included!

text: More Expertise, More Support: Why Your Pet Benefits from Credentialed Veterinary Technicians | Veterinary Dermatology Center
More Expertise, More Support: Why Your Pet Benefits from Credentialed Veterinary Technicians
» More Expertise More Support Why Your Pet Benefits From Credentialed Veterinary Technicians

When you bring your pet to the veterinary clinic, you want knowledgeable people who care about your animal as much as you do. You also want someone who listens, answers questions, and helps you feel supported. Credentialed Veterinary Technologists and Technicians (CrVTs) bring both technical expertise and compassion to your pet’s care team.

Next week is National Veterinary technician week in the United States and Canada dedicates all of October to celebrate credentialed veterinary technicians. So, it’s a great time to get to know these skilled professionals and the difference they make for pets and their families.

Those extra letters (CVT, LVT, RVT, LVMT) represent a serious commitment to animal health. CrVTs complete an accredited education program, pass a Veterinary Technician Licensing Exam, and continue learning to maintain their registration.

For your pet, that means having another trained professional involved in their care. Whether a visit involves dental treatment, another procedure requiring anesthesia, or other care, a CrVT brings knowledge and technical skills vital for your pet’s health.
Support for your pet and you

A CrVT’s contribution also includes attention to your pet’s comfort. Through gentle handling that aims to reduce stress and assessment of pain management, CrVTs help support animal welfare during veterinary care.

They also help care for the person holding the leash or carrier. Explaining pet care and offering nutrition advice are part of the CrVT’s role. If you have questions about your pet’s daily care, ask how a CrVT can help. A conversation can be an opportunity to discuss what feels manageable at home and where you need more guidance.
A team with a range of skills

Veterinary care brings together many kinds of expertise. CrVTs contribute knowledge in areas including laboratory science, X-rays, nutrition, anesthesia and emergency care. They also support disease prevention through work such as parasite testing and infection control.

Some CrVTs work beyond the familiar clinic setting, contributing to animal health through research, education, shelter medicine, and wildlife care. Their profession reaches well beyond the moments you see during an appointment.
Get to know your pet’s CrVT

This October, if you don’t already have a relationship with them, ask your veterinary clinic to introduce you to its CrVTs. Find out how they contribute to your pet’s care and what support they can offer you.
Having a CrVT on the team brings together skilled care for your pet and compassionate support for your family. That is something worth recognizing all year.

headings: Don’t Save That Concern for Your Pet’s Next Checkup
A wellness exam already has a full agenda
“While we’re here…” can deserve a visit of its own
Waiting can also cost your pet comfort
Keep the list—just don’t use it as a waiting room
text: Don’t Save That Concern for Your Pet’s Next Checkup | Veterinary Dermatology Center
Don’t Save That Concern for Your Pet’s Next Checkup
» Dont Save That Concern For Your Pets Next Checkup
Your pet’s wellness exam is next month, and you have started a mental list: the ear scratching, the occasional limp, that change in appetite.
“I’ll ask about it at the checkup,” you think.

It is understandable. Life is busy, and combining everything into one visit seems practical. But saving up concerns can delay attention to a problem—and leave less time for the preventive care your pet’s wellness visit was meant to cover.
A wellness exam already has a full agenda

Even when your pet seems healthy, there is plenty to discuss. A wellness visit gives your veterinarian time to review daily habits, assess nutrition and weight, check teeth and mobility, discuss parasite protection, and recommend appropriate screening tests. Vaccinations are just one part of the visit.
Think of it as a chance to look at the whole picture: how your pet is doing now and what might help keep them healthy in the months ahead.
That appointment, however, has a set amount of time. When several new problems arrive along with your pet, the agenda changes.
“While we’re here…” can deserve a visit of its own
An itchy ear or a change in bathroom habits may sound like a quick question. But a short description does not always lead to a quick answer.

Your veterinarian may need to ask when the change started, how often it happens, and whether anything else has changed. Then comes a closer examination and, sometimes, testing. What looks like one small concern at home can require a more detailed investigation.
Your pet deserves that attention. The challenge is fitting it into time already reserved for a full wellness assessment.

The team may need to prioritize the most pressing concern and arrange another appointment for other problems or preventive care. Discussions about food, oral health, or screening tests may need to wait.
It is a little like setting aside time to plan your weekly meals, then discovering the refrigerator has stopped working. The immediate problem naturally takes over.
Waiting can also cost your pet comfort

Pets cannot tell us exactly how they feel, and early signs of illness may be subtle. A change that seems minor can be worth investigating before it becomes more obvious. Detecting some conditions earlier gives veterinarians a chance to manage them before more serious problems develop.
This does not mean every scratch requires an urgent appointment. It means you do not have to decide on your own whether a change can safely wait.
Call your veterinary team when you notice a concern. Explain what you are seeing and when it started. They can help determine the next step and appropriate timing.
If a wellness appointment is already booked, let the clinic know about new concerns beforehand. For example:
“My dog is booked for a checkup next week, but she has started scratching her ear. Should she be seen sooner, and will we need a separate appointment?”
That information helps the team plan. Depending on the concern and availability, they may recommend an earlier visit, allow more time, or book a separate appointment.
And if you remember something only once you are in the exam room, speak up. The goal is never to keep concerns to yourself. It is to give each concern the time it needs.
Keep the list—just don’t use it as a waiting room
Notes about your pet’s habits and questions are excellent things to bring to a wellness exam. But a list works best as a memory aid, not a place to park health problems until the next checkup.
This October, for Pet Wellness Month, make two habits part of your pet’s care: keep regular wellness appointments, and contact your veterinary team when something changes.
That way, your pet gets timely attention for today’s concerns—and dedicated time to plan for tomorrow’s health.

Their lifestyle helps shape the plan
There is more to that exam than meets the eye
Blood and urine tell another part of the story
Make room for wellness this October
text: More Than a Shot: What Your Pet’s Wellness Visit Can Uncover | Veterinary Dermatology Center
More Than a Shot: What Your Pet’s Wellness Visit Can Uncover
» More Than A Shot What Your Pets Wellness Visit Can Uncover
If your pet could write the review, a veterinary visit might get three stars: “Excellent treats. Questionable thermometer. Would prefer the park.”
But while your pet is keeping track of the snacks, your veterinarian is gathering clues about their health.

October is Pet Wellness Month—a great reminder that routine veterinary visits are for much more than vaccinations. Vaccines provide important protection, but a wellness visit also includes a conversation about daily life, a physical exam, and recommendations tailored to your pet. Even when no vaccines are due, there is plenty worth checking.

You know your pet’s routines: the breakfast dance, the favorite sleeping spot, the very firm opinion about dinner being five minutes late. That makes your observations an important part of their care.

Your veterinarian will ask about eating, drinking, bathroom habits, activity, and behavior. Mention changes, even if they seem small: more trips to the water bowl, less enthusiasm for walks, or different litter box habits. Pets cannot explain how they feel, and early signs of illness can be subtle. Your everyday observations help your veterinarian decide what needs a closer look.

There is no need to arrive with a diagnosis. “Something seems different” is a useful place to start. And don’t forget home videos – pets act differently in clinic than at home so if you’re seeing anything unusual, take a video to show to your vet.
Their lifestyle helps shape the plan
Is your dog an outdoor adventurer or a dedicated couch companion? Does your cat stay indoors or explore the neighborhood?

Questions about your pet’s lifestyle help your veterinarian tailor their care. Food, exercise, parasite prevention, dental care, and weight management all belong in this conversation. It is also your chance to ask questions: Are those portions right? What should you do about toothbrushing? How can you support your pet’s changing needs?
Think of it as a planning session for your pet’s everyday well-being—with someone who will happily discuss both poop and portion sizes.
There is more to that exam than meets the eye
Some parts of a physical exam are easy to recognize. Others may look like your veterinarian is simply giving your pet a friendly once-over. Those hands, eyes, and ears are working.
During an exam, your veterinarian can check for:
, including extra body fat or muscle loss.
, such as inflamed gums or broken teeth.
These findings may point to a problem that needs further investigation. An exam helps your veterinarian work out what to check next; it does not always provide the whole answer on its own.
Blood and urine tell another part of the story
Your pet may look healthy, eat well, and still have early changes happening inside their body. Wellness testing can help uncover some of those changes before obvious signs appear.
Checks red blood cells, which carry oxygen; white blood cells, which respond to infection and inflammation; and platelets, which help blood clot.
Measures substances in the blood that provide clues about organs and body processes. Results can help identify possible kidney or liver problems, diabetes, and other conditions.
Examines urine for clues about kidney and urinary tract health. It can also help identify signs of diabetes or urinary inflammation. Blood and urine results work together to give a fuller picture.
Yes, that little cup of pee has a surprisingly important job.

Testing does not have to uncover a problem to be valuable. Results collected while your pet is well provide a starting point for future comparisons. Over time, your veterinarian can look for changes and patterns that help guide care.
An abnormal result is not always a diagnosis, either. Your veterinarian may recommend repeating a test or investigating further, depending on the finding.

Your pet’s age, health, and individual risks help determine which tests make sense and how often to perform them. Finding a problem earlier may allow treatment or monitoring to begin before it causes more serious difficulties.
Make room for wellness this October

Bring your questions, your observations, and details about what your pet eats—including the extras. Ask the clinic beforehand whether you should bring a sample or follow any instructions before testing.
This Pet Wellness Month, schedule a wellness visit and ask what care fits your pet’s needs. Your pet can focus on the treats. You and your veterinary team can focus on helping them feel their best.

title: Stronger Together: How One Rabies Vaccine Protects a Community | Veterinary Dermatology Center
headings: Stronger Together: How One Rabies Vaccine Protects a Community
An old disease with a preventable outcome
Your veterinarian helps protect people, too
Being a good neighbor can start with your pet
One choice can strengthen the whole safety net
text: Stronger Together: How One Rabies Vaccine Protects a Community | Veterinary Dermatology Center
Stronger Together: How One Rabies Vaccine Protects a Community
» Stronger Together How One Rabies Vaccine Protects A Community
What if one of the best things you do for your neighbors this year happens at your pet’s veterinary visit?

When your dog, cat, or ferret gets a rabies vaccine, the protection doesn’t stop at your front door. It reaches your family, other pets, the veterinary team, and people you may never meet. One simple appointment becomes part of a much larger safety net.
That is the idea behind this year’s World Rabies Day theme:
An old disease with a preventable outcome

Rabies is one of the world’s oldest recorded diseases. People wrote about its frightening effects thousands of years ago. Today, we know that rabies is caused by a virus. It attacks the brain and spinal cord and can infect any mammal. It most often spreads through saliva after a bite or scratch.
We also know how to prevent it.

Once signs of rabies appear, the disease is almost always fatal – even in 2026. Yet human deaths from rabies can be prevented. Vaccinating animals helps protect them and stop the disease spreading to people. Quick medical care including vaccination after a possible exposure can protect people before they become sick.

Working together has made a huge difference. Dog-related rabies is now mostly under control in the Americas. Some countries have ended it as a public health problem. Others have declared that they are free of rabies. Vaccination programs played a major role in that success.

This progress did not come from one person or one program. It came from many groups working toward the same goal. These groups include pet owners, veterinarians, doctors, public health teams, wildlife experts, shelters, and governments.

We’re not done yet. Rabies continues to cause tens of thousands of human deaths each year. Most happen in parts of Asia and Africa and children are most often affected. Dogs are linked to up to 99% of human rabies cases around the world. Many people at risk have limited access to dog vaccines and urgent medical care.

Rabies tells two stories at once. It shows how much we can achieve together. It also reminds us that our work is not finished. We can’t forget how deadly Rabies can be if effective vaccination programs aren’t regularly used.
Your veterinarian helps protect people, too
We often think of human and animal health as two separate areas. Doctors care for people, while veterinarians care for animals. Rabies shows us why the two are closely linked.

Veterinarians protect human health when they vaccinate pets. They also guide families after a pet meets a wild animal. They watch for signs of rabies and report concerns to public health officials. Doctors and public health teams then help people who may have been exposed.
. It means that the health of people, animals, and the places we share are connected. Rabies prevention is a clear example of One Health at work.

Indoor pets are part of this picture, too. A cat may slip through an open door. A dog may meet wildlife in the yard. A bat may enter a home and attract a curious cat or ferret. The level of risk depends on where you live and what your pet does. However, living indoors doesn’t mean there is no risk.

Keeping your pet’s rabies vaccine up to date can make a big difference after a possible exposure. Vaccinated pets may face fewer or shorter limits on their movement. Local rules differ, so ask your veterinarian what is required where you live.
Being a good neighbor can start with your pet
“Stronger Together” is a worldwide message. It also applies close to home. Here are some ways you can help:

Ask your veterinarian when your dog, cat, or ferret is due. Indoor pets may still need protection. Like any medicine, a vaccine can cause side effects. Most are mild and short-lived, but more serious reactions can happen. Tell your veterinarian if your pet has reacted to a vaccine before. Your veterinary team can help choose the safest plan for your pet.
You may need it after a bite, escape, or contact with wildlife.
Use a leash or secure outdoor area. Fix gaps in fences and screens. These steps protect pets, wildlife, and neighbors.

Never touch a bat or other wild mammal. This includes animals that seem injured, friendly, or easy to catch. Keep pets away and call local animal control, wildlife services, or public health for advice.
Act quickly after a possible human exposure.
Wash bites and scratches right away with soap and running water for at least 15 minutes. Get medical advice and contact local public health. Do not wait for signs of illness.
Call your veterinarian after a possible pet exposure.
Do this if your pet fights with, mouths, or is bitten by a wild or unknown animal. Keep the animals apart if you can do so safely. Do not touch them with bare hands.

Support trusted shelters, rescue groups, and local vaccine programs. Share information from trusted veterinary and public health sources. Listen to questions without judgment and encourage concerned pet owners to speak with their veterinarian.
One choice can strengthen the whole safety net
No pet owner can end rabies alone. Neither can one veterinarian, doctor, shelter, or public health team. Each person and group is one part of the safety net.

Your pet’s vaccine helps protect your home. Your choices help protect your neighborhood. Strong neighborhoods help build healthier communities. Working together can move the world closer to ending human deaths from dog-related rabies.

On September 28, think about the power of that connection. A rabies certificate may look like a simple piece of paper. In fact, it stands for something much bigger. It shows that people and health professionals are choosing to protect one another.
Against rabies, we truly are stronger together.

Why is my veterinarian referring my pet to the Veterinary Dermatology Center?

The fees you pay for veterinary services take into consideration a number of factors, including the costs to compensate your veterinarian and veterinary team for their professional services and the expenses involved in maintaining the hospital and equipment. When someone decides to adopt a pet, he or she needs to be prepared to include annual veterinary care in the overall cost of owning the pet.

Thanks to advances in veterinary medicine, pets are living longer, which means you may be spending more over the lifetime of your pet. However, in general, the annual cost of caring for a pet hasn’t increased much over the past several decades. (Consider how much the costs of many professional services, such as human healthcare, have risen over that same period!) Certain advanced procedures may come at a higher cost, but as the owner, you decide what care you want to provide your pet. Overall, veterinary care is a terrific value for pet owners.

It may seem like you’re paying more for your pet’s care than for your own, but that perception may stem from the fact that you’re paying the entire cost of a service or procedure, rather than a percentage or set fee determined by an insurance company. If you want to save money on your pet’s care, there are several pet insurance plans available. These plans may cover or help keep costs down for many routine veterinary services, prescriptions, medical conditions, and diseases. Your veterinary hospital may also offer a third-party healthcare line of credit as an option. Be sure to ask at your hospital if they accept any of these plans.

title: Anesthesia and Patient Monitoring – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: Anesthesia and Patient Monitoring – Veterinary Dermatology Center

Making sure our patients remain safe during surgery and other medical procedures is extremely important to us. Our team of veterinarians and veterinary technicians is skilled in using anesthesia and monitoring patients to ensure their safety and provide the most comfortable experience. Anesthesia and patient monitoring vary greatly from clinic to clinic. You can be confident that we use the most effective and up-to-date protocols. The type of anesthesia we use depends on the procedure. Some require general anesthesia, while others may only call for local anesthesia. We also closely monitor every procedure, regardless of whether it’s routine or more advanced. For more specific information on our protocols, please see the individual descriptions or contact us with any questions.

We monitor our patients closely to keep them as safe as possible during procedures that require general anesthesia. A veterinary technician will continually assess your pet’s heart and respiratory rate, blood pressure, and other vital signs to help prevent any anesthetic risk.
Please feel free to ask us about our patient monitoring protocol or any concerns you might have about your pet’s procedure. We’d be happy to discuss these matters in more detail.

For some procedures, your pet will need to be administered general anesthesia so that he or she will be unconscious and not feel pain. Many pet owners worry about their pets being administered general anesthesia. We can assure you that modern anesthesia is generally quite safe; to further lower any risk, we perform a physical examination and run blood work ahead of time to catch any underlying health issues. In addition, we follow a specific anesthetic protocol, including monitoring vital signs during the procedure, to ensure the safety of our patients.

We begin most general anesthetic procedures by administering a sedative to help the pet relax and decrease any anxiety and pain. We then administer an intravenous drug to provide complete anesthesia and place a breathing tube into the patient’s trachea (windpipe). To maintain the state of unconsciousness, we deliver a gas anesthetic in combination with oxygen through the breathing tube.
Please contact us if you have any questions or concerns about your pet receiving general anesthesia or about the procedure for which your pet is scheduled.

If your pet is having a minor surgical or diagnostic procedure performed, we sometimes use a local anesthetic to help control pain. For example, when we perform a biopsy (in which a small portion of tissue is surgically removed so it can be examined), we often use a local anesthetic. Local anesthetics cause a loss of sensation in the area where the procedure is being performed. We sometimes use a sedative and/or anxiolytic (anti-anxiety medication) in combination with the local anesthetic to keep pets calm during a procedure.
Please contact us if you have any questions or concerns about your pet receiving local anesthesia or about the procedure for which your pet is scheduled.

title: Medical Services – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: If your pet has ear, skin or allergy issues you can feel confident turning to us. Our knowledgeable doctors and staff are prepared to handle a wide variety of dermatological conditions. Please take a look at the more detailed descriptions of medical services we offer, or call us to discuss your pet’s needs.

Skin problems are common in dogs and cats and can be caused by pollen allergies, secondary infections, hormonal disorders, or parasites such as fleas and mites. These issues can be particularly difficult to treat and should be addressed promptly.

We can often diagnose a skin problem by simply examining your pet. Some dermatological diseases or conditions do require additional diagnostic procedures to ensure a correct diagnosis. Depending on your pet’s symptoms and the results of our physical exam, we may run blood work and/or perform cytology, skin scraping, cultures or biopsies.
Contact us if you notice your dog or cat scratching excessively or if he or she develops any bare patches, scabs, scaling, redness, inflammation, lumps, or bumps.

Identifying endocrine problems as early as possible is important in dogs and cats. These serious, potentially life-threatening conditions are much more manageable when caught early, allowing us to begin proper treatment.

The endocrine system is made up of a group of tissues (mostly glands) that release hormones into the bloodstream. These hormones regulate metabolism, growth, development, and reproduction and are dispersed to different areas of the body, depending on the hormone’s function. When a hormonal balance is disturbed (by a tumor or autoimmune disease, for instance), an endocrine disorder can develop. “Hyper” refers to an excess of hormone, and “hypo” refers to a deficiency in a hormone. Treatment varies depending on the disease.
There are several common endocrine disorders found in dogs and cats:
Diabetes mellitus is caused by a deficiency in or resistance to the hormone insulin.
Hypothyroidism, which is often diagnosed in dogs, indicates that the animal has low levels of thyroid hormone.
Hyperthyroidism, which frequently affects cats, indicates that the animal has high levels of thyroid hormones.
Addison’s disease (hypoadrenocorticism) and Cushing’s disease (hyperadrenocorticism) can also affect both species, although Cushing’s disease is rare in cats.

Contact us if your pet begins panting excessively, develops any skin issues (such as hair loss or dull coat), or shows any changes in behavior, energy levels, appetite, weight, water consumption, or urination.

title: Preventive Services – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: A simple way you can help keep your pet healthy is by protecting him or her against parasites. Heartworms, fleas, ticks, and other internal and external parasites are much more than just pests; they can cause life-threatening conditions in your pet—and cause severe, potentially fatal, health problems for you and your family. We will recommend the best preventive regimen for your pet, based on lifestyle and risk factors. We can also provide expert advice on keeping your whole household safe from parasitic infection. Set up an appointment with us to discuss parasite prevention, or call us to refill your pet’s medication. Protect your pet and your family today!

Fleas can cause problems for pets ranging from minor to life-threatening. Not only can these parasites cause severe itching, irritation, and allergies, but they can also transmit tapeworms and diseases. Fleas can infest dogs, cats, ferrets, mice, and rats. And fleas don’t just stay on pets; they can bite people, too. For more information, contact us or see the flea article in the Pet Health Library on our site.

You don’t want these blood-sucking parasites on your pet or in your home. We can help keep them away or help you get rid of them if they’ve already found their way inside. Call us to find out how to eliminate and control fleas or to start your pet on a preventive today.

Ticks are becoming more and more prevalent in North America, and they’re now being found in areas where people and pets didn’t previously encounter ticks. These parasites aren’t just a nuisance; they can cause serious—and sometimes deadly—diseases, including Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis, and tick paralysis. Contact us immediately if your pet starts coughing or has joint pain, trouble breathing, fever, weakness, or loss of appetite, weight, energy, or coordination.

The best method for keeping ticks off your pet is by keeping your dog or cat on a tick preventive. Even indoor-only pets are at risk because ticks can hitch a ride inside on your clothing or shoes. Tick preventives are safe and highly effective at controlling ticks and the diseases they carry. Call us to get your pet protected today!

Don’t panic if you find a tick on your dog or cat, even if your pet is on a preventive. Some preventives kill ticks after they’ve come in contact with your pet. Ticks can hide easily under your pet’s fur, so as an added measure of protection, we recommend checking your pet for ticks every time your pet comes in from outside. And don’t hesitate to ask us any questions you might have.

title: How to give eye ointment to your cat – Veterinary Dermatology Center
headings: How to give eye ointment to your cat
text: How to give eye ointment to your cat – Veterinary Dermatology Center
How to give eye ointment to your cat
» How to give eye ointment to your cat

Your cat is prescribed eye ointment. Here’s how you apply it. Start by washing your hands to prevent contamination and avoid spreading the infection. Gently clean any debris from your cat’s eyes with warm water and a washcloth. Take the tube and hold it in your hands briefly to warm and soften the ointment. Squeeze the tube like toothpaste so the ointment is near the tip, but don’t remove the cap yet.

There are different ways to position your cat when applying eye ointment. One way is to hold the cat in your lap facing away from you. Another is to sit beside them, something that might work if your cat doesn’t like being held. If needed, you can try wrapping them in a towel, leaving only their head exposed. You may even decide to have someone else hold your cat while you give the medication.

Now that you’ve got your cat in a comfortable position, hold the tube between your thumb and index finger with the tip pointed downward with your other hand. Gently tilt your cat’s head up. You can gently rest the hand holding the tube on your cat’s head for stability, and then use your available fingers and thumb to spread the top and bottom eyelids.

Hold the tube tip close to your cat’s eye, but do not touch the eye surface with the applicator. Squeeze the prescribed amount of ointment directly onto the eyeball, aiming for the center of the eye or into the pocket created by lifting the lid. You may need to close your cat’s eyelid to get the ointment to release from the tube.

Blinking will naturally spread the medication over their eye. If your cat is struggling, you can release them. Otherwise, reward them with massage and treats. Here’s a few extra pieces of advice. Now that you’ve got your dog in a comfortable position, hold the bottle between your thumb and index finger with the tip pointed downward with your other hand. Gently tilt your dog’s head up. You can gently rest the hand holding the bottle on your dog’s head for stability and then use your available fingers and thumb to spread the top and bottom eyelids.

Hold the bottle close to your dog’s eye, but do not touch the eyes. Surface with the applicator. Squeeze the prescribed number of drops directly onto the eyeball, aiming for the center of the eye. Blinking will naturally spread the medication over their eye. If your dog is struggling, you can release them. Otherwise, reward them with massage and treats. Here’s a few extra tips.

It’s important to keep the medication applicator. Tip two. Don’t let it come in contact with your dog, their eye, or any other surface. If you think you miss getting a drop in your dog’s eye or aren’t really sure, just give another one. The odd extra drop won’t make a difference. And lastly, take it as slow as you need to give yourself and your dog time to work through this process.

Here are the key things to remember when giving eye drops. Find a position that’s comfortable. Keep the applicator tip clean and praise your dog when it’s over. Giving eye drops can be tricky and may not go as planned, but you do the best you can because your dog is worth it.

title: Preventive Services – Veterinary Dermatology Center
text: A simple way you can help keep your pet healthy is by protecting him or her against parasites. Heartworms, fleas, ticks, and other internal and external parasites are much more than just pests; they can cause life-threatening conditions in your pet—and cause severe, potentially fatal, health problems for you and your family. We will recommend the best preventive regimen for your pet, based on lifestyle and risk factors. We can also provide expert advice on keeping your whole household safe from parasitic infection. Set up an appointment with us to discuss parasite prevention, or call us to refill your pet’s medication. Protect your pet and your family today!

Fleas can cause problems for pets ranging from minor to life-threatening. Not only can these parasites cause severe itching, irritation, and allergies, but they can also transmit tapeworms and diseases. Fleas can infest dogs, cats, ferrets, mice, and rats. And fleas don’t just stay on pets; they can bite people, too. For more information, contact us or see the flea article in the Pet Health Library on our site.

You don’t want these blood-sucking parasites on your pet or in your home. We can help keep them away or help you get rid of them if they’ve already found their way inside. Call us to find out how to eliminate and control fleas or to start your pet on a preventive today.

Ticks are becoming more and more prevalent in North America, and they’re now being found in areas where people and pets didn’t previously encounter ticks. These parasites aren’t just a nuisance; they can cause serious—and sometimes deadly—diseases, including Lyme disease, Rocky Mountain spotted fever, babesiosis, ehrlichiosis, and tick paralysis. Contact us immediately if your pet starts coughing or has joint pain, trouble breathing, fever, weakness, or loss of appetite, weight, energy, or coordination.

The best method for keeping ticks off your pet is by keeping your dog or cat on a tick preventive. Even indoor-only pets are at risk because ticks can hitch a ride inside on your clothing or shoes. Tick preventives are safe and highly effective at controlling ticks and the diseases they carry. Call us to get your pet protected today!

Don’t panic if you find a tick on your dog or cat, even if your pet is on a preventive. Some preventives kill ticks after they’ve come in contact with your pet. Ticks can hide easily under your pet’s fur, so as an added measure of protection, we recommend checking your pet for ticks every time your pet comes in from outside. And don’t hesitate to ask us any questions you might have.
